title: Acute cholecystitis: diagnosis, severity and timing of cholecystectomy

guidelineVersions: GIRFT Delivering an emergency gallbladder service (July 2026)

brief.role: Core surgical trainee in general surgery
brief.scenario: Mrs Angela Quinlan, 52, has had constant right upper quadrant pain for 36 hours. Temperature 38.2°C, pulse 96. She catches her breath when you press under the right costal margin. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a thickened gallbladder wall.
brief.task: Discuss the diagnosis and management of her condition with the examiner.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Diagnose with the Tokyo criteria, grade severity, then plan early surgery.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Planning to 'cool it down' and list her for surgery in six weeks.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is acute calculous cholecystitis: local signs, systemic signs and imaging all fit."

grid.label: Diagnosis
grid.fail: Calls it biliary colic, or diagnoses on pain alone.
grid.pass: Tokyo criteria: local signs (Murphy's sign, RUQ pain or mass), systemic signs (fever, raised CRP or white count) and imaging: definite cholecystitis.
grid.high: Checks liver function and duct diameter to look for bile duct stones or cholangitis before planning surgery.

grid.label: Severity grading
grid.fail: Does not grade severity, or treats every case the same.
grid.pass: Grade III: organ dysfunction. Grade II: white count above 18, tender RUQ mass, over 72 hours, or marked local inflammation. Grade I: neither.
grid.high: Grades her as Grade I and uses grade, comorbidity and fitness to choose early surgery or drainage.

grid.label: Initial treatment
grid.fail: Discharges her with oral analgesia, or gives no antibiotics.
grid.pass: Admits; analgesia, IV fluids, blood cultures and IV antibiotics per local policy; bloods including LFTs, lipase or amylase.
grid.high: Watches for deterioration to Grade III or cholangitis, and escalates to a senior if organ dysfunction develops.

grid.label: Timing of surgery
grid.fail: Plans to settle her and list for interval cholecystectomy at six weeks.
grid.pass: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis (NICE).
grid.high: Knows national GIRFT guidance now makes cholecystectomy during the index admission the default, rather than interval surgery.

grid.label: Consent and safe surgery
grid.fail: Does not mention bile duct injury or conversion.
grid.pass: Consents for bleeding, bile leak, bile duct injury, retained stones and conversion to open; critical view of safety before dividing structures.
grid.high: Knows bail-out options if the critical view cannot be achieved: subtotal cholecystectomy (fenestrating or reconstituting) or conversion.

grid.label: The unfit patient
grid.fail: Operates regardless of fitness, or has no plan for a patient too sick for surgery.
grid.pass: Antibiotics and percutaneous cholecystostomy as a bridge if too unwell for surgery; reconsider cholecystectomy when fit.
grid.high: Cites NICE: cholecystostomy for empyema when surgery is contraindicated and conservative treatment fails; involves seniors and critical care in the decision.

fail.text: I wouldn't grade it; all cholecystitis is treated the same.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Acute calculous cholecystitis. By the Tokyo criteria she has a local sign, a positive Murphy's; systemic signs, fever; and ultrasound findings. That's a definite diagnosis.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Grade III has organ dysfunction. Grade II has a white count over 18, a tender mass, symptoms over 72 hours or marked local inflammation. Otherwise Grade I.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Admit her, analgesia, IV fluids, blood cultures and IV antibiotics per local policy, and bloods including liver function.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: When should her gallbladder come out?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: NICE says early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What would you consent her for?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Bleeding, bile leak, bile duct injury, retained stones and conversion to open. I'd achieve the critical view of safety before dividing anything.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What if she were too unwell for surgery?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Antibiotics and a percutaneous cholecystostomy as a bridge, then reconsider cholecystectomy when she's fit.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Her LFTs come back normal and the duct is 5 mm.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Good, that makes duct stones and cholangitis less likely, so I can plan cholecystectomy without an MRCP first.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Grade I: no organ dysfunction and none of the Grade II features. With her fitness that points to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She becomes hypotensive and confused overnight.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's organ dysfunction, so now Grade III. I'd resuscitate, escalate to my registrar and consultant, and involve critical care.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: GIRFT's July 2026 guidance makes cholecystectomy during the index admission the default. Delaying surgery leads to 20 to 30% readmissions.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: In theatre you cannot get a critical view.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd bail out rather than push on: subtotal cholecystectomy, fenestrating or reconstituting, or conversion, with senior help.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: NICE reserves cholecystostomy for empyema when surgery is contraindicated and conservative treatment fails. Tokyo allows surgery for Grade III only in advanced centres with strict criteria.

failures.move: Settling the attack and listing for interval surgery.
failures.consequence: Readmission with recurrent cholecystitis, pancreatitis or duct stones, and a harder operation later.

failures.move: Not checking liver function or duct diameter.
failures.consequence: Bile duct stones or cholangitis are missed before surgery.

failures.move: Dividing structures without a critical view of safety.
failures.consequence: Risk of common bile duct injury.

failures.move: Operating on a patient with organ dysfunction outside a specialist setting.
failures.consequence: High perioperative risk when drainage could bridge her to safer surgery.

recovery.line: Early: within a week of diagnosis, ideally during this admission.
No critical view, no division: I'd bail out with a subtotal cholecystectomy or convert.

knowledge.fact: Tokyo diagnosis: local signs plus systemic signs plus imaging = definite.
Grade III: organ dysfunction. Grade II: white count over 18, tender RUQ mass, over 72 hours, or marked local inflammation.
Offer early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis.
Cholecystectomy during the index admission is the default; delayed surgery brings 20–30% readmissions.
Critical view of safety before dividing any structure; subtotal cholecystectomy as a bail-out.
Cholecystostomy for empyema when surgery is contraindicated and conservative treatment fails.

recall.think: Empyema, perforation, cholangitis, and bile duct injury at surgery.
recall.trap: 'Cool it down and operate in six weeks.'
recall.finish: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy with a critical view of safety; cholecystostomy if unfit.

media.task: Describe the ultrasound findings that support acute cholecystitis
media.description: Right upper quadrant ultrasound showing gallstones with acoustic shadowing, a thickened gallbladder wall and a small rim of pericholecystic fluid; common bile duct not dilated

partner.opening: Here is her ultrasound report. What is going on, and how would you manage her?

reveals.finding: WCC 15, CRP 140, bilirubin, ALP and ALT normal, amylase normal.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the bile duct on ultrasound
reveals.finding: Common bile duct 5 mm, no duct stones seen.

push.question: What severity grade is she?
push.expect: Grade I: no organ dysfunction, none of the Grade II features.

push.question: When should she have her cholecystectomy?
push.expect: Within 1 week of diagnosis; index admission by default.

push.question: What would you consent her for?
push.expect: Bleeding, bile leak, duct injury, retained stones, conversion; critical view of safety.

push.question: What if she were too unwell for surgery?
push.expect: Antibiotics and percutaneous cholecystostomy as a bridge.

curveballs.prompt: Her bilirubin is 60 and the duct is 10 mm.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Suspect duct stones: MRCP, and clear the duct by ERCP or at surgery alongside cholecystectomy.

curveballs.prompt: She is 88, on noradrenaline in ICU, with an empyema.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Grade III: percutaneous cholecystostomy as a bridge; reconsider surgery when she recovers.

curveballs.prompt: The next list is five days away.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Still within a week of diagnosis; keep her in and do it this admission rather than discharge.
